The second used test footage of a hen's egg set to part of Goldsmith's ''Alien'' score.<ref name="McIntee, 40" /> The film was previewed in various American cities in the spring of 1979<ref name="McIntee, 40" /> and was promoted with the [[tagline]] "In space no one can hear you scream",<ref name="nightmare fulfilled" /><ref name="Allrovi overview">{{cite web |title=Alien |publisher=[[Allrovi]] |url=http://www.allrovi.com/movies/movie/alien-v1503 |access-date=July 2, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110731155143/http://www.allrovi.com/movies/movie/alien-v1503 |archive-date=July 31, 2011}}</ref> which was written by [[Barbara Gips]], husband of [[Philip Gips]], who designed the poster.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Longman |first=Jeré |date=27 October 2025 |title=Barbara Gips, 89, Creator of Movie Catchphrases That Could Be as Memorable as the Films |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/10/24/movies/barbara-gips-dead.html |access-date=2025-12-06 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref>

''Alien'' was [[Motion Picture Association of America film rating system|rated "R"]] in the United States, "[[History of British film certificates#1970–1982|X]]" in the United Kingdom, and "[[Australian Classification Board#Film and video game classifications|M]]" in Australia.<ref name="McIntee, 14" /> In the UK, the [[British Board of Film Classification|British Board of Film Censors]] almost passed the film as an "AA" (for ages 14 and over), although concerns existed over the prevalent sexual imagery. 20th Century-Fox eventually relented in pushing for an AA certificate after deciding that an X rating would make it easier to sell as a horror film.<ref name="BBFC">{{cite web |url=https://darkroom.bbfc.co.uk/original/40d09668df091cfc0a32835f35c3674e:bc144b65f7d4e9f9243b495e7515609f/alien-report.pdf |title=Alien: BBFC classification report |publisher=[[BBFC]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130313202054/http://www.bbfc.co.uk/sites/default/files/attachments/Alien-Final.pdf |archive-date=March 13, 2013 |url-status=live |access-date=November 7, 2018}}</ref>

''Alien'' had its world premiere as a midnight screening on May 24, 1979, at the [[Seattle International Film Festival]]<ref>{{cite web |url=https://issuu.com/siffnews/docs/fest1979_catalog/13 |title= Seattle International Film Festival 1979 Catalog |date= March 24, 2024 |access-date=2025-05-13}}</ref> and opened in a [[limited release]] in American theaters on May 25.<ref name="Allrovi overview" /><ref>{{cite web |last=Ross |first=Jane |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-film-alien-anniversary/sigourney-weaver-marks-alien-anniversary-i-thought-it-was-a-small-movie-idUSKCN1ST2PA |title=Sigourney Weaver marks 'Alien' anniversary: 'I thought it was a small movie' |date=May 23, 2019 |publisher=Reuters|access-date=June 23, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190624033453/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-film-alien-anniversary/sigourney-weaver-marks-alien-anniversary-i-thought-it-was-a-small-movie-idUSKCN1ST2PA|archive-date=June 24, 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> Moviegoers lined up for blocks to see the film at [[Grauman's Egyptian Theatre]] in [[Hollywood, Los Angeles|Hollywood]], where a number of models, sets, and props were displayed outside to promote it during its first run.<ref name="McIntee, 40" /><ref name="nightmare fulfilled" /> It received a [[wide release]] in the United States on June 22.<ref>{{cite web |last=Illuminati |first=Chris |url=https://brobible.com/entertainment/article/alien-movie-facts/ |title='Alien' Was Released 37 Years Ago This Week — Here Are Some Crazy Facts Only True Fans Know About The Film |date=June 20, 2016 |website=BroBible|access-date=June 23, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190624033457/https://brobible.com/entertainment/article/alien-movie-facts/|archive-date=June 24, 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> Vandals [[Arson|set fire]] to the model of the space jockey, believing it to be the work of the [[devil]].<ref name="McIntee, 40" /> The film started its international release in Japan on July 20 and then Brazil on August 20.<ref name=foreign /> In the United Kingdom, ''Alien'' premiered at a gala performance at the 33rd [[Edinburgh International Film Festival]] on September 1, 1979,<ref>{{cite news |title=Something nasty lurking amid the good old Alien corn: Derek Malcolm reviews the new films in London and Edinburgh |first=Derek |last=Malcolm |newspaper=[[The Guardian]] |date=September 6, 1979 |author-link=Derek Malcolm}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://ftvdb.bfi.org.uk/sift/event/2261 |title=33rd Edinburgh International Film Festival |work=[[British Film Institute]] |publisher=BFI (Online Database) |access-date=August 20, 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120802222547/http://ftvdb.bfi.org.uk/sift/event/2261 |archive-date=August 2, 2012}}</ref> before starting an exclusive run at the [[Odeon Leicester Square]] in London on Thursday, September 6, 1979,<ref>{{cite magazine |magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |title=Japan & Britain Launch For 'Alien' |date=June 13, 1979 |page=24}}</ref> for one week before expanding slowly until opening wide in Britain in 180 theaters on October 1, 1979.<ref name=foreign>{{cite magazine |magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |title=Fox's 'Alien' Wows Alien Filmgoers |date=October 10, 1979 |page=28}}</ref> The film opened in France and Spain in September before expanding to other markets in October 1979.<ref name=foreign />

=== Box office ===
The film was a commercial success, opening in 90 theaters across the United States (plus 1 in Canada), setting 51 house records and grossing $3,527,881 over the four-day [[Memorial Day]] weekend with a per-screen average of $38,767,<ref name="box office mojo" /> which ''[[Daily Variety]]'' suggested may have been the biggest per-screen opening in history.<ref>{{cite magazine |magazine=[[Daily Variety]] |page=1 |last=Pollock |first=Dale |title=Per-Screen 'Alien' B.O. May Be Record |date=May 30, 1979}}</ref> It was the [[List of 1979 box office number-one films in the United States|number one film in the United States]] where it remained for three weeks.<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|title=50 Top-Grossing Films|url=https://archive.org/details/sim_variety_1979-06-20_295_7/page/9|date=June 20, 1979|page=9}}</ref> In its first 4 weeks it grossed $16.5&nbsp;million from only 148 prints before expanding to 635 screens.<ref name="box office mojo" /> In the UK, the film opened at the [[Odeon Leicester Square]] in London and grossed [[Pound sterling|£]]71,988 in its opening week, the biggest opening week of all-time for any cinema in the UK, to become the number one film in the UK.<ref>{{cite magazine |magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |page=41 |title='Alien' Bows In Britain |date=September 12, 1979}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=[[Screen International]]|date=September 15, 1979|page=2|title=London Box Office|last=Brown|first=Chris}}</ref> It remained at number one for eight weeks.<ref name=guinness>{{cite book |last1=Swern |first1=Phil |title=The Guinness Book of Box Office Hits |date=1995 |publisher=Guinness Publishing Ltd |isbn=0-85112-670-7 |page=437|url=https://archive.org/details/guinnessbookofbo0000swer/page/437/mode/1up?view=theater|via=[[Internet Archive]]}}</ref>
By the beginning of October 1979, the film had grossed $27 million internationally including $16.9 million in Japan, $4.8 million in France and $3.7 million in the UK.<ref name=foreign /> It went on to gross $78.9&nbsp;million in the United States and [[Pound sterling|£]]7,886,000 in the United Kingdom during its first run.<ref name="McIntee, 40" /> Including reissues, it has grossed $81.8&nbsp;million in the United States and Canada, while international box-office figures have varied from $24&nbsp;million to $122.7&nbsp;million. Its total worldwide gross has been listed within the range of $109.7&nbsp;million<ref name="box office mojo" /> to $188&nbsp;million.<ref name="numbers" /> In 1992, Fox noted the worldwide gross was $143&nbsp;million.<ref>{{cite magazine |magazine=[[Daily Variety]] |title=The Baddest of Them All (Fox advertisement) |page=8 |date=October 6, 1992}}</ref>

20th Century Fox claimed that ''Alien'' lost $2&nbsp;million in the 11 months following its release. The claim was decried by industry accountants as an example of [[Hollywood accounting|Hollywood creative accounting]], used to disguise the revenue and limit any payments to Brandywine. By August 1980, Fox readjusted the figure to $4&nbsp;million profit, although this was similarly refuted. Eager to begin work on a sequel, Brandywine sued Fox over their profit distribution tactics, but Fox claimed that ''Alien'' was not a financial success and did not warrant a sequel. The lawsuit was settled in 1983 when Fox agreed to fund a sequel.<ref name="Macek2015">{{cite magazine |last=Macek |first=J.C. III |date=May 12, 2015 |title=Hollywood Creative Accounting, or, How to Hide a Hit and Still Profit From It |url=https://www.popmatters.com/192246-hollywood-creative-accounting-or-how-to-hide-a-hit-and-still-profit--2495541881.html |url-status=live |magazine=[[PopMatters]] |oclc=1122752384 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230204131532/https://www.popmatters.com/192246-hollywood-creative-accounting-or-how-to-hide-a-hit-and-still-profit--2495541881.html |archive-date=February 4, 2023 |access-date=May 9, 2024}}</ref>

=== Critical reception ===
Critical reaction to ''Alien'' was initially mixed. Some critics who were not usually favorable towards science fiction, such as [[Barry Norman]] of the [[BBC]]'s ''Film'' series, were positive about the film's merits.<ref name="McIntee, 40" /> Others, however, were not; reviews by ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'', ''[[Sight and Sound]]'', [[Vincent Canby]], and [[Leonard Maltin]]{{efn|Maltin reassessed the film upon the release of the Director's Cut and gave ''Alien'' a positive review.<ref>{{cite web |last=Christopher |first=Rob |url=http://chicagoist.com/2013/09/17/leonard_maltin_talks_about_45_years.php |title=Interview: Leonard Maltin Discusses 45 Years Of His Movie Guide |publisher=Chicagoist |date=September 17, 2013 |access-date=October 12, 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130926063011/http://chicagoist.com/2013/09/17/leonard_maltin_talks_about_45_years.php |archive-date=September 26, 2013}}</ref>}} were mixed or negative.<ref>{{cite web |title=Anti Reviews on Movie-Film-Review |publisher=[[Christopher Tookey]] |url=http://www.movie-film-review.com/devfilm.asp?rtype=3&id=387 |access-date=October 11, 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100727104752/http://www.movie-film-review.com/devfilm.asp?rtype=3&id=387 |archive-date=July 27, 2010}}</ref> A review by ''[[Time Out (company)|Time Out]]'' said the film was an "empty bag of tricks whose production values and expensive trickery cannot disguise imaginative poverty".<ref name="halliwell">{{cite book |last1=Halliwell |first1=Leslie |editor-first=John |editor-last=Walker |title=Halliwell's Film & Video Guide 2001 |location=London |publisher=[[HarperCollins]] |year=2001 |page=16 |isbn=0-00-653219-5 |edition=16th}}</ref> In their original review on ''[[Sneak Previews]]'', critics [[Gene Siskel]] and [[Roger Ebert]] gave the film "two 'yes' votes." Ebert called it "one of the scariest old-fashioned space operas I can remember." Siskel agreed that it was scary but said it was basically a "haunted house film" set "in a spaceship" and was "not the greatest science fiction film ever made."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.imdb.com/video/vi3037575961 |title=Sneak Previews Season 1 Episode 18 |publisher=IMDB |access-date=September 12, 2020 |archive-date=November 14, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201114044802/https://www.imdb.com/video/vi3037575961 |url-status=live}}</ref> Siskel gave the film three stars out of four in his original print review, calling it "an accomplished piece of scary entertainment" and praising Sigourney Weaver as "an actress who should become a major star," but listed among the film's disappointments that "[f]or me, the final shape of the alien was the least scary of its forms."<ref>[[Gene Siskel|Siskel, Gene]] (May 25, 1979). "Faint praise: Alien' succeeds in the scare department". ''[[Chicago Tribune]]''. Section 3, p. 2.</ref>

== Post-release ==
=== Home video ===
''Alien'' has been released in many [[home video]] formats and packages over the years. The first of these was a 17-minute [[Super 8&nbsp;mm film|Super-8]] version for home projectionists.<ref name="McIntee, 39" /> It was also released on both [[VHS]] and [[Betamax]] for [[video rental|rental]], which grossed it an additional $40,300,000 in the United States alone.<ref name="McIntee, 40" /> Several VHS releases were subsequently issued both separately and as [[box set|boxed sets]]. [[LaserDisc]] and [[Videodisc]] versions followed, including deleted scenes and director commentary as bonus features.<ref name="McIntee, 39" /><ref name="McIntee, 259">McIntee, 259.</ref> A VHS box set containing ''Alien'' and its sequels ''Aliens'' and ''Alien 3'' was released in facehugger-shaped boxes, and included some of the deleted scenes from the Laserdisc editions.<ref name="McIntee, 259" /> In addition, all three films were released on [[THX]] certified widescreen VHS releases in 1997.<ref>{{cite news |last=Seeber |first=Ken |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/southern-illinoisan-aliens-released/98855854/ |title='Alien'(s) released in Widescreen Series|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240126154255/https://www.newspapers.com/article/southern-illinoisan-aliens-released/98855854/ |date=December 4, 1997 |access-date=January 26, 2024 |archive-date=January 26, 2024 |page=20 |publisher=[[The Southern Illinoisan|Southern Illinoisan]] |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |url-status=live}} {{Open access}}</ref> When ''Alien Resurrection'' premiered in theaters that year, another set of the first three films was released including a ''Making of Alien Resurrection'' tape. A few months later, the set was re-released with the full version of ''Alien Resurrection'' taking the place of the making-of video.<ref name="McIntee, 259" /> ''Alien'' was released on [[DVD]] in 1999, both separately and, as ''The Alien Legacy'', packaged with ''Aliens'', ''Alien 3'' and ''Alien Resurrection''.<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://ew.com/article/1999/06/04/more-aliens-come-vhs-and-dvd/ |title=More "Aliens" come to VHS and DVD |author=Sauter, Michael |date=June 4, 1999 |magazine=Entertainment Weekly |access-date=September 25, 2012 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121013043956/http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,273583,00.html |archive-date=October 13, 2012}}</ref> This set, which was also released in a VHS version, included a commentary track by Ridley Scott.<ref name="McIntee, 39" /><ref name="McIntee, 259" /> The first three films of the series have also been packaged as the ''Alien Triple Pack''.

{{quote box|quote="The traditional definition of the term 'Director's Cut' suggests the restoration of a director's original picture, free of any creative limitations. It suggests that the filmmaker has finally overcome the interference of heavy-handed studio executives, and that the film has been restored to its original, untampered form. Such is not the case with ''Alien'': The Director's Cut. It's a completely different beast."<ref name="quadrilogy" /> |source=—Ridley Scott |align=right |salign=right |width=25%}}

==== Director's Cut ====
In 2003, 20th Century Fox was preparing the ''Alien Quadrilogy'' DVD box set, which would include ''Alien'' and its three sequels. In addition, the set would also include alternative versions of all four films in the form of "special editions" and "[[director's cut]]s". Fox approached Scott to digitally restore and remaster ''Alien'', and to restore original scenes which had been cut during the editing process for inclusion in an expanded version of the film.<ref name="quadrilogy">{{Cite AV media |people=[[Ridley Scott]] ([[Film director|Director]]) |date=December 2, 2003 |title=[[Alien Quadrilogy]] |medium=DVD booklet |publisher=[[20th Century Fox]] Home Entertainment, Inc |location=Los Angeles}}</ref> Upon viewing the expanded version, Scott felt that it was too long and chose to recut it into a more streamlined alternative version:
{{blockquote|
Upon viewing the proposed expanded version of the film, I felt that the cut was simply too long and the pacing completely thrown off. After all, I cut those scenes out for a reason back in 1979. However, in the interest of giving the fans a new experience with ''Alien'', I figured there had to be an appropriate middle ground. I chose to go in and recut that proposed long version into a more streamlined and polished alternate version of the film. For marketing purposes, this version is being called "The Director's Cut."<ref name="quadrilogy" />
}}
The "Director's Cut" restored around four minutes of deleted footage, while cutting about five minutes of other material, leaving it about a minute shorter than the theatrical cut.<ref name="McIntee, 40">McIntee, 40.</ref> Many of the changes were minor, such as new sound effects, trimming of some shots to speed up the film's pace and the removal of the "What Are My Chances?" scene. The restored footage included the scene in which Ripley discovers the cocooned Dallas and Brett during her escape of the ''Nostromo''. Fox released the Director's Cut in theaters on October 31, 2003.<ref name="McIntee, 40" /> The ''Alien Quadrilogy'' boxed set was released December 2, 2003, with both versions of the film included along with a new commentary track featuring many of the film's actors, writers, and production staff, as well as other special features and a documentary entitled ''The Beast Within: The Making of Alien''. Each film was also released separately as a DVD with both versions of the film included. Scott noted that he was very pleased with the original theatrical cut of ''Alien'', saying that "For all intents and purposes, I felt that the original cut of ''Alien'' was perfect. I still feel that way", and that the original 1979 theatrical version "remains my version of choice".<ref name="quadrilogy" /> He has since stated that he considers both versions "director's cuts", as he feels that the 1979 version was the best he could possibly have made it at the time.<ref name="quadrilogy" />

The ''Alien Quadrilogy'' set earned ''Alien'' a number of new awards and nominations. It won DVDX Exclusive Awards for Best Audio Commentary and Best Overall DVD, Classic Movie, and was also nominated for Best Behind-the-Scenes Program and Best Menu Design.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.imdb.com/event/ev0001644/2003/2/ |title=DVD Exclusive Awards 2003 |website=[[IMDb]] |access-date=September 1, 2022}}</ref> It also won a [[Saturn Award]] for Best DVD, and was nominated for Best DVD Collection and Golden [[Satellite Award]]s for Best DVD Extras and Best Overall DVD.<ref>{{cite web |title=The 2004 8th Annual SATELLITE™ Awards Nominees |url=http://www.pressacademy.com/satawards/ipa-satelliteawards-nominees.html |publisher=International Press Academy |accessdate=December 25, 2021 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20040402023056/http://www.pressacademy.com/satawards/ipa-satelliteawards-nominees.html |archivedate=April 2, 2004}}</ref> In 2010 both the theatrical version and Director's Cut of ''Alien'' were released on [[Blu-ray Disc]], as a stand-alone release and as part of the ''Alien Anthology'' set.<ref name="Empire">{{cite web |url=https://www.empireonline.com/news/story.asp?NID=28371 |title=Alien Series Has A Blu-ray Release Date |access-date=May 28, 2012 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121116170108/http://www.empireonline.com/news/story.asp?NID=28371 |archive-date=November 16, 2012}}</ref>

In 2014, to mark the film's 35th anniversary, a special re-release boxed set named ''Alien: 35th Anniversary Edition'', containing the film on [[Blu-ray]], a [[digital copy]], a reprint of ''Alien: The Illustrated Story'', and a series of collectible art cards containing artwork by H.R. Giger related to the film, was released.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://geeksofdoom.com/2014/09/12/alien-35th-anniversary-blu-ray-edition-coming-this-fall |title='Alien' 35th Anniversary Blu-ray Edition Coming This Fall |first=Adam |last=Frazier |date=September 12, 2014|access-date=September 1, 2022}}</ref> A [[soundtrack album]] was released, featuring selections of Goldsmith's score. Additionally, a [[single (music)|single]] of the Main Theme was released in 1980,<ref name="McIntee, 38-39">McIntee, 38–39.</ref> and a disco single using audio excerpts from the film was released in 1979 on the UK label [[Bronze Records]] by a recording artist under the name ''Nostromo''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.discogs.com/release/241603-Nostromo-Alien |title=Nostromo – Alien (1979, Vinyl) |date=September 21, 1979 |publisher=[[Discogs]]|access-date=September 1, 2022}}</ref> ''Alien'' was re-released on [[Ultra HD Blu-ray]] and 4K digital download on April 23, 2019, in honor of the film's 40th anniversary.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.highdefdigest.com/news/show/20th_Century_Fox/Disc_Announcements/Ridley_Scott/4K/alien-4k-ultra-hd-bluray-dated/43592 |title=ALIEN 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray Dated {{!}} High-Def Digest|website=www.highdefdigest.com|access-date=February 13, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190214002903/https://www.highdefdigest.com/news/show/20th_Century_Fox/Disc_Announcements/Ridley_Scott/4K/alien-4k-ultra-hd-bluray-dated/43592|archive-date=February 14, 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> The 4k Blu-ray Disc presents the film in 2160p resolution with [[HDR10]] [[high-dynamic-range video]]. Several previously released bonus features on the 4k Blu-ray include audio commentary from director Ridley Scott, cast and crew, the final isolated theatrical score and composer's original isolated score by Jerry Goldsmith, and deleted and extended scenes.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://hd-report.com/reviews/alien-1979-4k-ultra-hd-blu-ray-review/ |title=Alien (1979) 4k Ultra HD Blu-ray Review |date=April 28, 2019 |website=hd-report.com|access-date=May 4, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190505020449/https://hd-report.com/reviews/alien-1979-4k-ultra-hd-blu-ray-review/|archive-date=May 5, 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Cinematic analysis ===
Critics have analyzed ''Alien''{{'s}} sexual overtones. The film is often cited as a major work of [[abjection]], as outlined by [[Julia Kristeva]] in her 1980 work ''[[Powers of Horror]]''. According to Kristeva, the abject refers to that which signifies the breakdown of conventional borders and rules. It confronts the subject with the fallibility of the human body and societal norms, and thus exposes how the supposedly sacred distinctions between what is Self and what is Other are arbitrary.<ref>Kristeva, Julia. [Powers of Horror: An Essay on Abjection]</ref> She suggests that this confrontation—often manifesting in excrement, bodily invasion, and corpses—is an inherently traumatic interruption of subjectivity, and thus all evidence of abjection is hidden in conventional society. Much of ''Alien''{{'s}} effectiveness as a work of horror has been attributed to its use of abject themes and imagery, a narrative strategy that has made Kristeva's abject a major framework for feminist and psychoanalytic critics such as Barbara Creed. Following Creed's assertion that the alien creature is a representation of the "monstrous-feminine as [[archaic mother]]",<ref name=":0">Creed, Barbara. "Alien and The Monstrous-Feminine." ''Alien Zone: Cultural Theory and Contemporary Science Fiction Cinema''. Ed. [[Annette Kuhn]]. London: Verso, 1990. 128-141.</ref> Ximena Gallardo C. and C. Jason Smith compared the facehugger's attack on Kane to a male rape and the chestburster scene to a form of violent birth, noting that the alien's [[phallic]] head and method of killing the crew members add to the sexual imagery.<ref>Gallardo C., Ximena and C. Jason Smith (2004).''[https://books.google.com/books?id=k_H3vLIRECgC Alien Woman: The Making of Lt. Ellen Ripley] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160512223750/https://books.google.com/books/about/Alien_Woman.html?id=k_H3vLIRECgC |date=May 12, 2016}}''. "Chapter 1: Men, Women, and an Alien Baby" 13-61. Continuum. {{ISBN|0-8264-1569-5}}.</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Gallardo C.|first=Ximena|url=http://reconstruction.eserver.org/043/gallardoc.htm|title="'Who Are You?: Alien/Woman as Posthuman Subject in Alien Resurrection|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100316221238/http://reconstruction.eserver.org/043/gallardoc.htm|archive-date=March 16, 2010}}</ref> Dan O'Bannon, who wrote the film's screenplay, has argued that the scene is a metaphor for the male fear of penetration, and that the "oral invasion" of Kane by the facehugger functions as "payback" for the many horror films in which sexually vulnerable women are attacked by male monsters.<ref>{{cite news |last=Kermode |first=Mark |title=All Fright on the Night |newspaper=[[The Observer]] |date=October 19, 2003 |url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2003/oct/19/features.review |access-date=May 29, 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131005115207/http://www.theguardian.com/film/2003/oct/19/features.review |archive-date=October 5, 2013}}</ref> David McIntee claims that "''Alien'' is a rape movie as much as ''[[Straw Dogs (1971 film)|Straw Dogs]]'' (1971) or ''[[I Spit on Your Grave]]'' (1978), or ''[[The Accused (1988 film)|The Accused]]'' (1988). On one level, it's about an intriguing alien threat. On one level it's about [[Parasites in fiction|parasitism]] and disease. And on the level that was most important to the writers and director, it's about sex, and reproduction by non-consensual means. And it's about this happening to a man."<ref name="McIntee, 43">McIntee, 43.</ref> He notes how the film plays on men's fear and misunderstanding of pregnancy and childbirth, while also giving women a glimpse into these fears.<ref name="McIntee, 43-44">McIntee, 43–44.</ref>

Alternatively, H.R. Giger's xenomorph design has been interpreted through the lens of "machinic modernism," an aesthetic movement reacting to industrialization and social upheaval, linked to proto-fascist ideology (New Cinemas 2023).<ref name="Eden 63–90">{{Cite journal |last=Eden |first=Michael |date=2023-06-01 |title=Seeing the xenomorph, Giger's alien in the context of machinic modernism |url=https://intellectdiscover.com/content/journals/10.1386/ncin_00048_1 |journal=New Cinemas: Journal of Contemporary Film |language=en |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=63–90 |doi=10.1386/ncin_00048_1 |issn=1474-2756|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The xenomorph embodies traits such as armoured aggression, zoomorphism, and hierarchical social organization, reflecting anti-humanist ideals that valorize violence and dominance. Eden contextualizes the creature alongside works by [[Wyndham Lewis]] and [[Jacob Epstein]], whose art similarly celebrated hardened, phallic forms as responses to modernity's destabilizing forces. The alien's role in the narrative—eliminating a flawed, liberal crew to pave the way for Ripley's emergent leadership—mirrors proto-fascist fantasies of elite replacement, where a "heroic" figure (Ripley) justifies authoritarian reorganization by contrast to both weak democracies (the crew) and totalitarian horrors (the xenomorphs).<ref name="Eden 63–90"/> This framing draws on insights of Professor Anne Quema who observed that 'Giger in particular, and the Gothic in general, belong to the twentieth century trend of anti-humanist representation of identity. This iconoclastic project has its roots in early European avant-gardism so that Epstein's [[Rock Drill (Jacob Epstein)|Rock-Drill]] [...] and Giger's biomechanoids are part of the same genealogy.' <ref>{{Cite journal |last=Quéma |first=Anne |date=2004 |title=The Gothic and the Fantastic in the Age of Digital Reproduction |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/article/689565 |journal=ESC: English Studies in Canada |volume=30 |issue=4 |pages=81–119 |doi=10.1353/esc.2004.0067 |issn=1913-4835|url-access=subscription }}</ref> These readings, challenge the view of the xenomorph as a purely feminist return of the repressed,<ref name=":0" /> or as a boundary-defying deconstructive symbol,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cohen |first=Jeffrey Jerome |title=Monster Culture (Seven Theses) |date=2020-01-15 |work= |pages=37–56 |url=https://doi.org/10.5749/j.ctvtv937f.5 |access-date=2025-05-22 |publisher=University of Minnesota Press|doi=10.5749/j.ctvtv937f.5 |isbn=978-1-4529-6039-5 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> instead framing it as a "[[vanishing mediator]]" that consolidates fascistic subjectivity through its phallic coherence and mythic violence.

Film analyst Lina Badley has written that the alien's design, with strong [[Sigmund Freud|Freudian]] sexual undertones, multiple phallic symbols, and overall feminine figure, provides an [[androgyny|androgynous]] image conforming to [[archetype|archetypal]] mappings and imageries in horror films that often redraw gender lines.<ref name="badley">{{cite book |last=Badley |first=Lina |title=Film, Horror, and the Body Fantastic: Contributions to the Study of Popular Culture |publisher=[[Greenwood Press]] |location=Westport, CT |year=1995 |page=120 |isbn=978-0-313-27523-4}}</ref> O'Bannon described the sexual imagery as overt and intentional: "I am going to put in every image I can think of to make the men in the audience cross their legs. Homosexual oral rape, birth. The thing lays its eggs down your throat, the whole number."<ref>{{cite web |last=Emerson |first=Jim |title=Prometheus: Alien origins: The skeleton beneath the exoskeleton |url=https://www.rogerebert.com/scanners/prometheus-alien-originsthe-skeleton-beneath-the-exoskeleton |website=RogerEbert.com |date=June 14, 2012 |access-date=September 10, 2021}}</ref>
