| caption2 = Some have argued the film's narrative details and visual design were inspired by those of the 1965 Italian film ''[[Planet of the Vampires]]'' ''(top)'', such as a scene in which the crew discovers a ruin containing giant alien skeletons.<ref name="PopMatters">{{cite web |title=PopMatters – Building the Perfect Star Beast: The Antecedents of 'Alien' |date=November 20, 2012 |url=https://www.popmatters.com/column/165516-building-the-perfect-star-beast-the-antecedents-of-alien/|access-date=January 4, 2014|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131118023020/http://www.popmatters.com/column/165516-building-the-perfect-star-beast-the-antecedents-of-alien/|archive-date=November 18, 2013}}</ref>
}}
''Alien''{{'s}} roots in earlier works of fiction have been analyzed and acknowledged extensively by critics. The film has been said to have much in common with B movies such as ''[[The Thing from Another World]]'' (1951),<ref name="ebert 2003 review" /><ref name="french">{{cite news |last=French |first=Philip |title=Alien (review) |newspaper=[[The Guardian]] |date=November 2, 2003 |url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/News_Story/Critic_Review/Observer_review/0,,1075900,00.html |access-date=July 15, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080604032720/http://film.guardian.co.uk/News_Story/Critic_Review/Observer_review/0%2C%2C1075900%2C00.html |archive-date=June 4, 2008 |url-status=live}}</ref> ''[[Creature from the Black Lagoon]]'' (1954),<ref>Maçek III, J.C. [https://www.popmatters.com/pm/column/165516-building-the-perfect-star-beast-the-antecedents-of-alien/ "Building the Perfect Star Beast: The Antecedents of 'Alien'."] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121127172302/http://www.popmatters.com/pm/column/165516-building-the-perfect-star-beast-the-antecedents-of-alien |date=November 27, 2012}} ''[[PopMatters]]'', November 21, 2012.</ref> ''[[It! The Terror from Beyond Space]]'' (1958),<ref name="McIntee, 19" /><ref name="mackinder review" /> ''[[Night of the Blood Beast]]'' (1958),<ref>{{cite web |last=Eggerston |first=Chris |url=https://bloody-disgusting.com/news/19353 |title=Not So Scary... Top Ten Worst Movie Monsters! |website=[[Bloody Disgusting]] |date=March 4, 2010 |access-date=November 12, 2016 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160811141458/http://bloody-disgusting.com/news/19353 |archive-date=August 11, 2016}}</ref> and ''[[Queen of Blood]]'' (1966),<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.terrortrap.com/interviews/curtisharrington/ |title=Retrospective in Terror: An Interview with Curtis Harrington – April 2005 |publisher=The Terror Trap |access-date=November 12, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170409110004/http://www.terrortrap.com/interviews/curtisharrington/ |archive-date=April 9, 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref>
as well as its fellow 1970s horror films ''[[Jaws (film)|Jaws]]'' (1975) and ''[[Halloween (1978 film)|Halloween]]'' (1978).<ref name="ebert 2003 review" /> Literary connections have also been suggested: Philip French of the ''Guardian'' has perceived thematic parallels with Agatha Christie's ''[[And Then There Were None]]'' (1939).<ref name="french" /> Many critics have also suggested that the film derives in part from [[A. E. van Vogt]]'s ''[[The Voyage of the Space Beagle]]'' (1950), particularly its stories "The Black Destroyer", in which a cat-like alien infiltrates the ship and hunts the crew, and "Discord in Scarlet", in which an alien implants parasitic eggs inside crew members which then hatch and eat their way out.<ref>McIntee, 19–20.</ref><ref>[[Kingsley Amis|Amis, Kingsley]] (1981), Introduction to ''The Golden Age of Science Fiction: An Anthology''; London: Hutchinson, pg 26.</ref> O'Bannon denies that this was a source of his inspiration for ''Alien''{{'s}} story.<ref name="McIntee, 20" /> Van Vogt in fact initiated a lawsuit against 20th Century Fox over the similarities, but Fox settled out of court.<ref>{{cite news |title=The Voyage of the Space Beagle |work=My Science Fiction Life |publisher=BBC |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/dna/mysciencefictionlife/A20258336 |access-date=August 2, 2008 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719123104/http://www.bbc.co.uk/dna/mysciencefictionlife/A20258336 |archive-date=July 19, 2011}}</ref>

Several critics have suggested that the film was inspired by Italian filmmaker [[Mario Bava]]'s [[Cult film|cult]] [[Cult following|classic]] ''[[Planet of the Vampires]]'' (1965), in both narrative details and visual design.<ref name="PM">{{cite web |url=https://www.popmatters.com/pm/column/165516-building-the-perfect-star-beast-the-antecedents-of-alien/ |work=[[PopMatters]] |date=November 21, 2012 |title=Building the Perfect Star Beast: The Antecedents of 'Alien' |first=J.C. |last=Maçek III|access-date=November 12, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121127172302/http://www.popmatters.com/pm/column/165516-building-the-perfect-star-beast-the-antecedents-of-alien|archive-date=November 27, 2012|url-status=live}}</ref> Rick Sanchez of [[IGN]] has noted the "striking resemblance"<ref name="dvd.ign.com">{{cite web |url=http://dvd.ign.com/articles/354/354551p1.html |title=Planet of the Vampires |last=Sanchez |first=Rick |date=February 27, 2002 |work=dvd review |publisher=IGN Entertainment, Inc. |page=1|access-date=April 10, 2012 |location=San Francisco|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050308015154/http://dvd.ign.com/articles/354/354551p1.html|archive-date=March 8, 2005}}</ref> between the two movies, especially in a celebrated sequence in which the crew discovers a ruin containing the skeletal remains of long-dead giant beings, and in the design and shots of the ship itself.<ref name="Frentzen" /> [[Cinefantastique]] also noted the remarkable similarities between these scenes and other minor parallels.<ref name="Frentzen">Frentzen, Jeffrey. ''Cinefantastique'' Magazine, Volume 8, Number 4, 1979, pgs. 24 – 25. "''Alien'': It! The Terror from Beyond the Planet of the Vampires"</ref> Robert Monell, on the DVD Maniacs website, observed that much of the conceptual design and some specific imagery in ''Alien'' "undoubtedly owes a great debt" to Bava's film.<ref>{{cite web |last=Monell |first=Robert |title=Planet of the Vampires |url=http://www.dvdmaniacs.net/Reviews/M-P/planet_of_the_vampires.html |publisher=DVD Maniacs |access-date=January 24, 2007 |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061218150252/http://www.dvdmaniacs.net/Reviews/M-P/planet_of_the_vampires.html<!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archive-date=December 18, 2006}}</ref> Despite these similarities, O'Bannon and Scott both claimed in a 1979 interview that they had not seen ''Planet of the Vampires'';<ref name="Carducci">Carducci, Mark Patrick and Lovell, Glenn. ''Cinefantastique'', Volume 9, Number 1, 1979, pp.10–39. "Making ''Alien'': Behind The Scenes"</ref> decades later, O'Bannon would admit: "I stole the giant skeleton from the ''Planet of the Vampires''."<ref name="Rinzler">J.W.Rinzler. ''The Making of Alien'', Titanbooks, 2019, page 22.</ref>

Writer [[David A. McIntee|David McIntee]], as well as reviewers for ''[[PopMatters]]'' and ''[[Den of Geek]]'', have noted similarities to the ''[[Doctor Who]]'' serial ''[[The Ark in Space]]'' (1975), in which an insectoid queen alien lays [[larva]]e inside humans which later eat their way out, a life cycle inspired by that of the [[Ichneumonoidea|ichneumon wasp]].<ref name="McIntee, 20" /><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.popmatters.com/169127-doctor-who-the-ark-in-space-special-edition-2495772781.html |title=There's some seriously scary ethno-violence in 'Doctor Who: The Ark in Space – Special Edition' |work=[[PopMatters]] |first=Marco |last=Lanzagorta |date=March 13, 2013 |access-date=October 9, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.denofgeek.com/movies/doctor-who-the-ark-in-space-special-edition-review/ |title=Doctor Who: The Ark In Space – Special Edition review |work=[[Den of Geek]] |first=Andrew |last=Blair |date=February 15, 2013 |access-date=October 9, 2021}}</ref> McIntee also noted similarities between the first half of the film, particularly in early versions of the script, to [[H. P. Lovecraft]]'s ''[[At the Mountains of Madness]]'', "not in storyline, but in dread-building mystery",<ref name="McIntee, 23">McIntee, 23.</ref> and calls the finished film "the best Lovecraftian movie ever made, without being a Lovecraft adaptation", due to its similarities in tone and atmosphere to Lovecraft's works.<ref name="McIntee, 41" /> In 2009, O'Bannon said the film was "strongly influenced, tone-wise, by Lovecraft, and one of the things it proved is that you can't adapt Lovecraft effectively without an extremely strong visual style ... What you need is a cinematic equivalent of Lovecraft's prose."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FG2JRNVji-8 |title=Dan O'Bannon H.P. Lovecraft Film Festival 2009 Howie Award, PART 1 |publisher=[[YouTube]] |date=October 29, 2009|access-date=December 25, 2012|url-status=live|archive-url=http://archive.wikiwix.com/cache/20150914120419/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FG2JRNVji-8|archive-date=September 14, 2015}}</ref> H. R. Giger has said he liked O'Bannon's initial ''Alien'' storyline "because I found it was in the vein of Lovecraft, one of my greatest sources of inspiration."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.littlegiger.com/articles/files/Cinefantastique_09_01.pdf |title=H. R. Giger – Alien Design |publisher=littlegiger.com |work=[[Cinefantastique]] |last=Levy |first=Frederic Albert|access-date=December 25, 2012|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140103061926/http://www.littlegiger.com/articles/files/Cinefantastique_09_01.pdf|archive-date=January 3, 2014}}</ref>

=== Audience research ===
Findings from an international audience research project conducted by staff from [[Aberystwyth University]], [[Northumbria University]] and [[University of East Anglia]] were published in 2016 by [[Palgrave Macmillan]] as ''Alien Audiences: Remembering and Evaluating a Classic Movie''. 1,125 people were surveyed about their memories and opinions of the film in order to test some of the theories offered by academics and critics about why the film became so popular and why it has endured for so long as a masterpiece. The study discusses memories of ''Alien'' in the cinema and on home video from the point of view of everyday audiences, describing how many fans share the film with their children and the shocking impact of the "chestburster" scene, among other things.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Barker |first1=Martin |last2=Egan |first2=Kate |last3=Ralph |first3=Sarah |last4=Phillips |first4=Tom |date=2016 |title=Alien Audiences: Remembering and Evaluating a Classic Movie |publisher=Palgrave Macmillan |isbn=978-1-137-53205-3}}</ref>

=== Re-release ===
For its 45th anniversary, ''Alien'' was re-released in theaters by [[20th Century Studios]] on April 26, 2024.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.fangoria.com/alien-in-theaters/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20240812154948/https://www.fangoria.com/alien-in-theaters/|work=[[Fangoria]]|title=The Original Alien Returns to Theaters This Month|date=April 16, 2024|last=Wampler|first=Scott|accessdate=March 4, 2025|archive-date=August 12, 2024}}</ref>

== Legacy ==
=== Critical reassessment ===
In a 1980 episode of ''[[Sneak Previews]]'' discussing science fiction films of the 1950s and 1970s, the reviewers were critical of ''Alien''. [[Roger Ebert]] reiterated [[Gene Siskel]]'s earlier opinion, stating that the film was "basically just an intergalactic haunted house thriller set inside a spaceship". He described it as one of several science fiction pictures that were "real disappointments" compared to ''Star Wars'', ''[[Close Encounters of the Third Kind]]'', and ''[[2001: A Space Odyssey (film)|2001: A Space Odyssey]]''. However, in both episodes Ebert singled out the early scene of the ''Nostromo''{{'s}} crew exploring the alien planet for praise, calling the scene "inspired", said that it showed "real imagination" and claimed that it transcended the rest of the film.<ref name="Sneak Previews">{{cite AV media |last1=Siskel |first1=Gene |author1-link=Gene Siskel |last2=Ebert |first2=Roger |author2-link=Roger Ebert |title=Invasion of the Outer Space Movies |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dMXDU8EWDzE |url-status=live |date=1980 |access-date=October 14, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200228044745/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dMXDU8EWDzE&gl=US&hl=en&has_verified=1&bpctr=9999999999 |archive-date=February 28, 2020}}</ref> Over two decades later, Ebert had revised his opinion, including the film on his [[The Great Movies|''Great Movies'' list]], where he gave it four stars and said it was "a great original".<ref>{{cite web |last=Ebert |first=Chaz |url=https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/great-movie-alien-1979 |title=Alien Movie Review & Film Summary (1979) |publisher=Roger Ebert |date=October 26, 2003 |access-date=October 12, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151026124801/http://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/great-movie-alien-1979 |archive-date=October 26, 2015}}</ref> In 1980, ''Alien'' was mentioned in ''[[Cinefantastique]]''{{'}}s chronological recap of the top films of the 1970s but was not included in the article's "Decade's Top Ten" list. [[Frederick S. Clarke]], the ''Cinefantastique'' editor, wrote that ''Alien'' was "an exercise in style, refreshingly adult in approach, wickedly grim and perverse, that manages to compensate for a lack of depth in both story and characters".<ref name="ClarkeCinefantastique">{{cite magazine |last=Clarke |first=Frederick S. |title=1970~1979 Decade Recap: The Seventies 1970~1979 |magazine=[[Cinefantastique]] |volume=9 |issue=3–4 |year=1980 |pages=72–73 |issn=0145-6032 |oclc=2757769}}</ref> In 1982, [[John Simon (critic)|John Simon]] of the ''[[National Review]]'' praised the cast, particularly Weaver, and the visual values. He wrote: "For fanciers of horror, among whose numbers I do not count myself, ''Alien'' is recommendable, provided they are free from hypocrisy and finicky stomachs".<ref>{{cite book |title=Reverse Angle: A Decade of American Film |url=https://archive.org/details/reverseangledeca0000simo|url-access=registration |last1=Simon |first1=John |publisher=Crown Publishers Inc. |year=1982 |page=[https://archive.org/details/reverseangledeca0000simo/page/385 385] |isbn=978-0-517-54471-6}}</ref>

Despite initial mixed reviews, ''Alien'' has received critical acclaim over the years, particularly for its realism and unique environment,<ref name="mackinder review" /> and is cited one of the best films of 1979.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/top/bestofrt/?year=1979 |title=Top 100 Movies of 1979 |website=[[Rotten Tomatoes]]|access-date=November 24, 2016|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161124230215/https://www.rottentomatoes.com/top/bestofrt/?year=1979|archive-date=November 24, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.listal.com/list/best-films-of-1979 |title=Best Films of 1979 list |website=Listal|access-date=November 24, 2016|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170207202400/http://www.listal.com/list/best-films-of-1979|archive-date=February 7, 2017}}</ref> It is seen as one of the most influential science-fiction films.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.thestar.com/entertainment/movies/2015/09/03/a-parasite-to-remember-why-alien-is-one-of-the-most-influential-movies-ever-made.html |title=Why Alien is one of the most influential movies ever made |website=[[The Toronto Star]] |first=Peter |last=Howell |date=September 3, 2015|access-date=November 24, 2016|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161124221555/https://www.thestar.com/entertainment/movies/2015/09/03/a-parasite-to-remember-why-alien-is-one-of-the-most-influential-movies-ever-made.html|archive-date=November 24, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://screenprism.com/insights/article/which-films-influenced-alien-and-how |title=Which films influenced "Alien" and how? |website=Screen Prism |first=Nolan |last=Moore |date=May 25, 2015|access-date=November 24, 2016|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161125044510/http://screenprism.com/insights/article/which-films-influenced-alien-and-how|archive-date=November 25, 2016}}</ref> It holds {{a or an|{{RT data|score}}}} rating on [[Rotten Tomatoes]], based on {{RT data|count}} reviews and an average rating of {{RT data|average}}. The website's critical consensus reads, "A modern classic, ''Alien'' blends science fiction, horror and bleak poetry into a seamless whole."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/alien |title=Alien (1979) |website=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |publisher=[[Fandango Media|Fandango]]|access-date={{RT data|access date}}|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170204135810/https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/alien|archive-date=February 4, 2017|url-status=live}}{{RT data|edit}}</ref> [[Metacritic]] reports a weighted average score of 89 out of 100 based on 34 critics, indicating "universal acclaim".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.metacritic.com/movie/alien-re-release |work=[[Metacritic]] |publisher=[[CBS Interactive]] |title=Alien Reviews |access-date=April 9, 2019 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141009124039/http://www.metacritic.com/movie/alien-re-release |archive-date=October 9, 2014}}</ref> ''[[Halliwell's Film Guide]]'' awarded it a full four stars, describing it as "a classic of suspense and art direction".<ref name="halliwell" /> Alan Jones of ''[[Radio Times]]'' awarded it five out of five, describing it as a "revolutionary 'haunted house in space' thrill-ride [...] stunning you with shock after shock", praising the "top-notch acting [...] and imaginative bio-mechanical production design", as well as "Ridley Scott's eye for detail and brilliant way of alternating false scares with genuine jolts, which help to create a seamless blend of gothic horror and harrowing science fiction".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.radiotimes.com/film/zwts/alien/ |title=Alien |work=[[Radio Times]] |first=Alan |last=Jones |access-date=October 9, 2021 }}{{Dead link|date=February 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

Critical interest in the film was re-ignited with the theatrical release of the "Director's Cut" in 2003. Roger Ebert ranked it among "the most influential of modern action pictures" and praised its pacing, atmosphere, and settings:
{{blockquote|One of the great strengths of ''Alien'' is its pacing. It takes its time. It waits. It allows silences (the majestic opening shots are underscored by Jerry Goldsmith with scarcely audible, far-off metallic chatterings). It suggests the enormity of the crew's discovery by building up to it with small steps: The interception of a signal (is it a warning or an [[SOS]]?). The descent to the extraterrestrial surface. The bitching by Brett and Parker, who are concerned only about collecting their shares. The masterstroke of the surface murk through which the crew members move, their helmet lights hardly penetrating the soup. The shadowy outline of the alien ship. The sight of the alien pilot, frozen in his command chair. The enormity of the discovery inside the ship ("It's full of ... leathery eggs ...").<ref name="ebert 2003 review"/>
}}
[[David A. McIntee]] praises ''Alien'' as "possibly the definitive combination of horror thriller with science fiction trappings." He notes that it is a horror film first and a science fiction film second, since science fiction normally explores issues of how humanity will develop under other circumstances. ''Alien'', on the other hand, focuses on the plight of people being attacked by a monster: "It's set on a spaceship in the future, but it's about people trying not to get eaten by a drooling monstrous animal. Worse, it's about them trying not to get raped by said drooling monstrous animal." Along with ''Halloween'' and ''[[Friday the 13th (1980 film)|Friday the 13th]]'' (1980), he describes it as a prototype for the [[slasher film]] genre: "The reason it's such a good movie, and wowed both the critics, who normally frown on the genre, and the casual cinema-goer, is that it is a distillation of everything that scares us in the movies." He also describes how the film appeals to a variety of audiences: "Fans of [[Alfred Hitchcock|Hitchcockian]] thrillers like it because it's moody and dark. Gorehounds like it for the chest-burster. Science fiction fans love the [[hard science fiction]] trappings and hardware. Men love the battle-for-survival element, and women love not being cast as the helpless victim."<ref name="McIntee, 42">McIntee, 42.</ref>

[[David Edelstein]] wrote, "''Alien'' remains the key text in the 'body horror' subgenre that flowered (or, depending on your viewpoint, festered) in the seventies, and Giger's designs covered all possible avenues of anxiety. Men traveled through vulva-like openings, got forcibly impregnated, and died giving birth to rampaging gooey vaginas dentate — how's that for future shock? This was truly what [[David Cronenberg]] would call 'the new flesh,' a dissolution of the boundaries between man and machine, machine and alien, and man and alien, with a psychosexual invasiveness that has never, thank God, been equaled."<ref name="Edelstein">{{cite web |last=Edelstein |first=David |title=Prometheus Review: More Than Just an Alien |publisher=vulture.com |url=https://www.vulture.com/2012/06/movie-review-prometheus-alien-prequel.html |access-date=June 13, 2012 |date=June 8, 2012 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120610175933/http://www.vulture.com/2012/06/movie-review-prometheus-alien-prequel.html |archive-date=June 10, 2012}}</ref>

In 2008, the [[American Film Institute]] ranked ''Alien'' the seventh-best science fiction film as part of ''[[AFI's 10 Top 10]]'', a [[CBS]] television special ranking the greatest movies in ten classic American film genres. The ranks were based on a [[opinion poll|poll]] of over 1,500 film artists, critics, and historians, with ''Alien'' ranking just above ''[[Terminator 2: Judgment Day]]'' (1991) and just below Scott's other science fiction film ''[[Blade Runner]]'' (1982).<ref name="AFI poll">{{cite web |title=AFI's 10 Top 10: Top 10 Sci-Fi |publisher=[[American Film Institute]] |url=http://www.afi.com/10top10/category.aspx?cat=7 |access-date=July 22, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140328081240/http://www.afi.com/10top10/category.aspx?cat=7 |archive-date=March 28, 2014 |url-status=live}}</ref> The same year, ''[[Empire (film magazine)|Empire]]'' named ''Alien'' the 33rd-greatest film, based on a poll of 10,200 readers, critics, and members of the film industry.<ref name="Empire 500">{{cite web |title=''Empire's'' The 500 Greatest Movies of All Time |publisher=[[Empire (magazine)|Empire]] magazine |date=October 3, 2008 |url=https://www.empireonline.com/movies/features/500-greatest-movies/ |access-date=July 27, 2020 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120310180609/http://www.empireonline.com/500/91.asp |archive-date=March 10, 2012}}</ref> In 2016, the [[Directors Guild of America]] ranked the film 64th on its list of ''The 80 Best-Directed Films'' since the Guild’s founding in 1936.<ref>{{Cite news |title=The 80 Best-Directed Films - |url=https://www.dga.org/craft/dgaq/all-articles/1602-spring-2016/80th-film-poll.aspx |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241226110741/https://www.dga.org/craft/dgaq/all-articles/1602-spring-2016/80th-film-poll.aspx |archive-date=2024-12-26 |access-date=2026-10-18 |work=[[Directors Guild of America]] |language=en}}</ref> In 2021, Phil Pirrello of [[Syfy]] named it the second-scariest science fiction film. He described it as a "groundbreaking science fiction classic" and "a movie so influential that it's hard to think of a time before ''Alien''".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.syfy.com/syfywire/scariest-sci-fi-movies-list-aliens-anniversary |title=The 25 scariest sci-fi movies ever made, from 'Aliens' to 'Invisible Man', ranked |work=[[Syfy]] |first=Phil |last=Pirrello |date=July 15, 2021 |access-date=October 9, 2021}}</ref>

=== Cultural influence ===
[[File:Paisley Abbey &quot;Xenomorph&quot; Gargoyle (10317339143) (cropped).jpg|thumb|[[Paisley Abbey]] "Alien" [[gargoyle]] ({{circa|1990}}) in [[Paisley, Renfrewshire|Paisley]], Scotland]]
{{Quote box |quote="The 1979 ''Alien'' is a much more cerebral movie than its sequels, with the characters (and the audience) genuinely engaged in curiosity about this weirdest of lifeforms... Unfortunately, the films it influenced studied its thrills but not its thinking."<ref name="ebert 2003 review" /> |source=—Film critic [[Roger Ebert]] on ''Alien''{{'}}s cinematic effect. |align=right |salign=right |width=25%}}
''Alien'' had both an immediate and long-term effect on the science fiction and horror genres. Shortly after its debut, [[Dan O'Bannon]] was sued by another writer named Jack Hammer for allegedly plagiarising a script entitled ''Black Space''. However, O'Bannon was able to prove that he had written his ''Alien'' script first.<ref name="McIntee, 40-41">McIntee, 40–41.</ref> In the wake of ''Alien''{{'s}} success, a number of other filmmakers imitated or adapted some of its elements, sometimes by using "Alien" in titles. One of the first was ''The Alien Dead'' (1979), which had its title changed at the last minute to cash in on ''Alien''{{'s}} popularity.<ref name="McIntee, 262">McIntee, 262.</ref> ''[[Contamination (film)|Contamination]]'' (1980) was initially going to be titled ''Alien 2'' until 20th Century Fox's lawyers contacted writer/director [[Luigi Cozzi]] and made him change it. The film built on ''Alien'' by having many similar creatures, which originated from large, slimy eggs, bursting from characters' chests.<ref name="McIntee, 262" /> An unauthorized sequel to ''Alien'', titled ''[[Alien 2: On Earth]]'', was released in 1980 and included alien creatures which incubate in humans. Other science fiction films of the time that borrowed elements from ''Alien'' include ''[[Galaxy of Terror]]'' (1981), ''[[Inseminoid]]'' (1981), ''[[Forbidden World]]'' (1982), ''[[Xtro]]'' (1982), and ''[[Dead Space (film)|Dead Space]]'' (1991).<ref name="McIntee, 262" />

The "chestburster" effect was parodied in [[Mel Brooks]]'s comedy ''[[Spaceballs]]''. Near the end, in a diner, John Hurt does a cameo appearance as a customer who seems to be suffering indigestion. He turns out to have an "alien" in his gut, and moans, "Oh, no...not again!" The "alien" then does a song-and-dance, singing a line of "Hello, Ma Baby", from the classic Warner Bros. cartoon ''[[One Froggy Evening]]''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.complex.com/pop-culture/2013/01/25-best-scenes-comedy-spoof-movies/spaceballs-chestburster |title=The 25 Best Scenes in Comedy Spoof Movies: 1. Chestburster song and dance number |website=Complex |access-date=March 30, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190330233346/https://www.complex.com/pop-culture/2013/01/25-best-scenes-comedy-spoof-movies/spaceballs-chestburster |archive-date=March 30, 2019 |url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Nintendo]]'s long-running ''[[Metroid]]'' video game series, created in 1986, was significantly influenced by ''Alien'', both in stylistic and thematic elements. As an homage to ''Alien'', villains in [[Metroid (video game)|the first ''Metroid'' installment]] were named Ridley and Mother Brain, after the movie's director and the ship computer, respectively.<ref>"The Making of Super Metroid". [[Retro Gamer]]. [[Imagine Publishing]] Ltd. (65): 60. July 2009.</ref>

Notably, at [[Paisley Abbey]], during a restoration project that took place in the 1990s, a stonemason from [[Edinburgh]] hired to replace twelve crumbling stone [[gargoyle]]s erected one bearing a strong resemblance to the space creature from the film.<ref>[https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/av/uk-scotland-23810978 BBC News Scotland] 'Alien' gargoyle on ancient abbey, August 23, 2013</ref><ref>{{citation |last=Did You Know ? |title=The Mystery Of Why There's An "Alien" Gargoyle On A 12th-Century Scottish Abbey May Have Been Solved |date=March 30, 2018 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UlQBfmjnAmw |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211221/UlQBfmjnAmw |archive-date=December 21, 2021 |url-status=live|access-date=April 11, 2018}}{{cbignore}}</ref> A picture of the gargoyle went viral in 2013, though a photograph of the statue first surfaced on the internet in 1997.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-scotland-glasgow-west-23810979 |title='Alien' gargoyle on ancient abbey |date=August 23, 2013 |publisher=BBC News|access-date=April 11, 2018 |language=en-GB}}</ref> In 2002, it was confirmed the abbey would undergo a 10-year-long restoration project.{{fact|date=May 2026}}

In [[SFR Yugoslavia]] the film and its sequels were distributed under the title ''Osmi putnik'' (transl. ''Eighth Traveller'').<ref name="kulturkokoska">{{cite web|first= Ivana |last= Adamović |title= Ko se boji tuđina još! |website= Kultur!Kokoška |date= 24 May 2017 |access-date= 3 August 2024 |url= https://kulturkokoska.rs/ko-se-boji-tudina-jos/}}</ref> The highly popular Yugoslav and later [[Croatia]]n [[hard rock]] band [[Osmi Putnik]] chose their name after the film.<ref name="janjatović">{{cite book|last=Janjatović|first=Petar|title=Ex YU rock enciklopedija 1960–2023|year=2024|publisher=self-released / Makart|location=Belgrade|page=218}}</ref>

In 2002, ''Alien'' was deemed "culturally, historically or aesthetically significant" by the [[National Film Preservation Board]] of the United States,<ref name="nfpb about">{{cite web |title=National Film Preservation Board |publisher=[[National Film Preservation Board]] |url=https://www.loc.gov/film/filmabou.html |access-date=September 6, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080829144823/http://www.loc.gov/film/filmabou.html |archive-date=August 29, 2008 |url-status=dead}}</ref> and was inducted into the [[National Film Registry]] of the [[Library of Congress]] for historical preservation alongside other films of 1979 including ''[[All That Jazz (film)|All That Jazz]]'', ''[[Apocalypse Now]]'', ''[[The Black Stallion (film)|The Black Stallion]]'', and ''[[Manhattan (1979 film)|Manhattan]]''.<ref name="national film registry">{{cite web |title=Films Selected to the National Film Registry, Library of Congress, 1989–2007 |publisher=[[National Film Registry]] |url=https://www.loc.gov/film/titles.html |access-date=September 6, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080829144902/http://www.loc.gov/film/titles.html |archive-date=August 29, 2008 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Librarian of Congress Adds 25 Films to National Film Registry |url=https://www.loc.gov/item/prn-02-176/librarian-of-congress-adds-25-films-to-national-film-registry/2002-12-17/ |access-date=September 14, 2020 |website=Library of Congress |archive-date=October 30, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201030133619/https://www.loc.gov/item/prn-02-176/librarian-of-congress-adds-25-films-to-national-film-registry/2002-12-17/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2019, author [[J. W. Rinzler]] published ''The Making of Alien'', a behind-the-scenes book about the making of the film with cast and crew interviews and previously unseen photographs. ''[[The Verge]]'' praised the book as "the definitive story of the classic horror film".<ref>{{cite web |last=Liptak |first=Andrew |title=J.W. Rinzler's The Making of Alien is the definitive story of the classic horror film |url=https://www.theverge.com/2019/8/4/20699924/j-w-rinzler-the-making-of-alien-definitive-behind-the-scenes-book-interview |website=The Verge |date=August 4, 2019 |access-date=August 6, 2021}}</ref>

[[Eli Roth]] cites ''Alien'' as his primary influence, saying "I saw ''Alien'' when I was 8 years old. To me, it was like a combination of ''Jaws'' and ''Star Wars'' and that's the movie that made me want to be a director. It traumatized me. I actually threw up I was so nervous after I saw it but that's like the highest compliment you can give a horror film."<ref>{{cite web |last=Nissim |first=Mayer |title=Eli Roth: 'Alien made me throw up' |url=https://www.digitalspy.com/movies/a273441/eli-roth-alien-made-me-throw-up/ |publisher=[[Digital Spy]] |date=September 6, 2010 |access-date=October 9, 2021}}</ref> [[Ty Franck]], one of the authors behind the sci-fi series ''[[The Expanse (TV series)|The Expanse]]'', credits ''Alien'' as one of his major inspirations.<ref>{{cite episode |title=''Alien'' and ''The Expanse'' Deep Dive |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZKuHsj8jMb8  |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211221/ZKuHsj8jMb8 |archive-date=December 21, 2021 |url-status=live|access-date=February 12, 2021 |series=Ty & That Guy |network=[[Amazon Studios]] |date=February 8, 2021 |minutes= |time= |transcript=|transcript-url= |quote= |via=[[YouTube]]}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

=== Merchandise ===
[[Alan Dean Foster]] wrote a novelization of the film in both adult and "junior" versions, which was adapted from the film's shooting script.<ref name="McIntee, 38" /> ''[[Heavy Metal (magazine)|Heavy Metal]]'' magazine published ''[[Alien: The Illustrated Story]]'', a [[graphic novel]] adaptation of the film scripted by [[Archie Goodwin (comics)|Archie Goodwin]] and drawn by [[Walt Simonson]], as well as a 1980 ''Alien'' [[calendar]].<ref name="McIntee, 38" /> Two behind-the-scenes books were released in 1979 to accompany the film. ''The Book of Alien'' contained many production photographs and details on the making of the film, while ''Giger's Alien'' contained much of H. R. Giger's concept artwork for the movie.<ref name="McIntee, 38" /> A [[scale model|model kit]] of the alien, 12 inches high, was released by the [[Model Products Corporation]] in the United States, and by [[Airfix]] in the United Kingdom.<ref name="McIntee, 39">McIntee, 39.</ref> [[Kenner]] also produced a larger-scale Alien action figure, as well as a board game in which players raced to be first to reach the shuttle pod while Aliens roamed the ''Nostromo''{{'s}} corridors and air shafts.<ref name="McIntee, 39" /> Official [[Halloween costume]]s of the alien were released in October 1979.<ref name="McIntee, 39" />

=== School play adaptation ===
In 2019, students at [[North Bergen High School]] in New Jersey adapted the film into a play. The production had no budget, with props and sets developed from recycled toys and other items. Social media recognition brought Scott's attention to the play. He wrote a letter of congratulations to the students ("My hat comes off to all of you for your creativity, imagination, and determination") and recommended they consider an adaptation of his film ''[[Gladiator (2000 film)|Gladiator]]'' for their next stage production.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.indiewire.com/2019/03/ridley-scott-writes-letter-praising-high-school-students-alien-production-1202054131/ |title=Ridley Scott Praises Students for 'Alien' Stage Show, Offers Funds for Encore Performance|first1=Zack|last1=Sharf|publisher=[[IndieWire]]|language=en-US|url-status=live|date=March 28, 2019|access-date=April 8, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190407152217/https://www.indiewire.com/2019/03/ridley-scott-writes-letter-praising-high-school-students-alien-production-1202054131/|archive-date=April 7, 2019}}</ref> He donated to the school to put on an encore performance at which Weaver was in attendance. She got on stage before the performance to congratulate the cast and crew for their creativity and commitment.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.cnn.com/2019/03/25/entertainment/alien-high-school-play/index.html |title=A high school's 'Alien' play is the talk of Hollywood |first=Lisa Respers |last=France|publisher=[[CNN]]|date=March 25, 2019|access-date=April 8, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190812103351/https://www.cnn.com/2019/03/25/entertainment/alien-high-school-play/index.html|archive-date=August 12, 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Video game adaptations ===
{{Main|Alien (1982 video game)|Alien (1984 video game)|Alien: Isolation}}
In 1982, Fox Video Games released an ''[[Alien (1982 video game)|Alien]]'' video game for the [[Atari 2600]]. With gameplay reminiscent of ''[[Pac-Man]]'', in it the player traverses a maze collecting items and destroying alien eggs, while avoiding the creature.<ref name=Prima>{{cite web|last=Buffa|first=Christopher|title=Alien Evolution - From Atari 2600 to PlayStation 4|url=https://www.primagames.com/games/alien-isolation/feature/alien-evolution-atari-2600-playstation-4|publisher=[[Prima Games]]|access-date=2017-09-10|date=2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170907124814/https://www.primagames.com/games/alien-isolation/feature/alien-evolution-atari-2600-playstation-4|archive-date=2017-09-07|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Argus Press Software]] made another game called ''[[Alien (1984 video game)|Alien]]'' in 1984 for the [[Commodore 64]], [[ZX Spectrum]], and [[Amstrad CPC]] computers, a straighter adaptation of the film where after Kane's death the player controls the crew of the ''Nostromo'' roaming the ship in search for the alien.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.thunderboltgames.com/feature/an-alien-retrospective|website=Thunderbolt Games|title=An Alien Retrospective|first=Pete|last=Worth|date=11 February 2013|accessdate=21 July 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150722041434/http://www.thunderboltgames.com/feature/an-alien-retrospective|archive-date=22 July 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|website=[[Polygon.com]]|url=http://www.polygon.com/2014/10/3/6892091/history-of-alien-games-aliens|title=From Atari to Isolation: A video and written history of Alien games|first1=Alexa Ray|last1=Corriea |first2=Danielle|last2=Riendeau|date =3 October 2014|accessdate=21 July 2015}}</ref>

The 2014 video game ''[[Alien: Isolation]]'', which serves as a partial sequel to ''Alien'' in featuring Ripley's daughter Amanda trying to find out the whereabouts of her mother 15 years after the destruction of the ''Nostromo'', had two downloadable content packs titled ''Crew Expendable'' and ''Last Survivor'' depicting alternate versions of key events from the film, with the original cast members Sigourney Weaver, Tom Skerrit, Veronica Cartwright, Harry Dean Stanton, and Yaphet Kotto reprising their respective roles.<ref>{{cite web |access-date=6 August 2015 |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2014/07/09/original-alien-cast-reunite-for-alien-isolation-dlc?+main+twitter |title=Original Alien Cast Reunite for Alien: Isolation DLC |website=[[IGN]] |author=Daniel Krupa |date=9 July 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150806200903/http://www.ign.com/articles/2014/07/09/original-alien-cast-reunite-for-alien-isolation-dlc?+main+twitter |archive-date=6 August 2015 |url-status=live}}</ref>

''Crew Expendable'' centers around the events of the movie after Brett's disappearance in the air ducts, prompting the crew to attempt to force the alien into the airlock. Unlike the film, where Dallas would be the first to attempt this while armed with a flamethrower, the game provides the player with the option to play as Ripley, Dallas, or Parker, which would result in the chosen character to enter the ducts first.

''Last Survivor'' focuses on the climax of the film, where Ripley is left to be the last crew member and proceeds to self-destruct the ''Nostromo''.

In 2023, an ''Alien'' Chapter DLC was released for the multiplayer asymmetrical horror game [[Dead by Daylight]]. It included the ''Xenomorph'' and ''Ellen Ripley'' as a playable Killer and Survivor, respectively. The Nostromo was added as a Map in the form of the ''Nostromo Wreckage'', where players can interact with the environment and spot Easter-eggs such as ''Jonesy the Cat'', and a ''Facehugger''. The Xenomorph's Power allows it to enter ''Crawler Mode'', where it runs on all fours, gains access to a Tail Attack, and becomes stealthier. Its secondary ability involves Tunnels that it can enter and travel quickly around the Map, gaining Crawler Mode quicker while inside them. Survivors are able to collect Flame Turrets from these tunnels, which, once placed down, can indicate if the Xenomorph is near, and will spew a stream of fire if it gets close enough, potentially forcing it out of Crawler Mode. The Xenomorph can destroy these turrets, which will force Survivors to collect new ones. Notable Cosmetics that players can buy and equip include the ''Xenomorph Queen'' from ''[[Aliens (film)|Aliens]]'', the ''Grid Xenomorph'' from ''[[Alien vs. Predator (film)|Alien vs. Predator]]'', a Human-Xenomorph Hybrid based on the ''Newborn'' from ''[[Alien Resurrection]]'', and Rain Carradine from ''[[Alien: Romulus]]'' as a Skin for Ripley. Sigourney Weaver's likeness was not used for Ellen Ripley, and neither did she voice the character.

== Sequels and franchise ==
{{further|Alien (franchise)}}
[[File:Sigourney Weaver by Gage Skidmore 4.jpg|thumb|264x264px|[[Sigourney Weaver]] became the star of the ''Alien'' films, reprising her role as Ripley in three sequels between 1986 and 1997. She did not appear in either of the ''Alien vs. Predator'' crossovers of the 2000s, but has expressed interest in doing a fifth ''Alien'' film.]]
The success of ''Alien'' led [[20th Century Fox]] to finance three direct [[sequel]]s over the next eighteen years, each by different writers and directors. [[Sigourney Weaver]] remained the only recurring actor through all four films: the story of her character [[Ellen Ripley|Ripley]]'s encounters with the [[Alien (Alien franchise)|aliens]] became the thematic and narrative core of the series.<ref name="ebert 2003 review" /> [[James Cameron]]'s ''[[Aliens (film)|Aliens]]'' (1986) focused more on action and involved Ripley returning to the planetoid accompanied by [[marine (military)|marines]] to confront hordes of aliens.<ref name="aliens" /> [[David Fincher]]'s ''[[Alien 3]]'' (1992) had [[nihilistic]] tones<ref name="McIntee, 41" /> and found her on a prison planet battling another Alien, ultimately sacrificing herself to prevent her employers from acquiring the creatures.<ref name="alien 3">{{cite AV media |people=[[David Fincher|Fincher, David]] (Director) |title=[[Alien 3]] |medium=[[DVD]] |publisher=[[20th Century Fox]] |location=Beverly Hills, CA |date=2003}}</ref> [[Jean-Pierre Jeunet]]'s ''[[Alien Resurrection]]'' (1997) saw Ripley resurrected through [[cloning]] to battle more aliens even further in the future.<ref name="alien resurrection">{{cite AV media |people=[[Jean-Pierre Jeunet|Jeunet, Jean-Pierre]] (Director) |title=[[Alien Resurrection]] |medium=[[DVD]] |publisher=[[20th Century Fox]] |location=Beverly Hills, CA |date=2003}}</ref>

The success of the film series resulted in the creation of a [[media franchise]] with numerous novels, comic books, video games, toys, and other media and merchandise appearing over the years. A number of these began appearing under the ''[[Alien vs. Predator]]'' [[fictional crossover|crossover]] imprint, which brought the alien creatures together with the eponymous characters of the [[Predator (franchise)|''Predator'' franchise]]. A film series followed, with ''[[Alien vs. Predator (film)|Alien vs. Predator]]'' in 2004, and ''[[Aliens vs. Predator: Requiem]]'' in 2007.<ref name="avp">{{cite AV media |people=[[Paul W. S. Anderson|Anderson, Paul W. S.]] (Director) |title=[[Alien vs. Predator (film)|Alien vs. Predator]] |medium=[[DVD]] |publisher=[[20th Century Fox]] |location=Beverly Hills, CA |date=2005}}</ref><ref name="avp:r">{{Cite AV media |people=[[Brothers Strause|Strause, Colin and Greg]] (Directors) |title=[[Aliens vs. Predator: Requiem]] |medium=[[DVD]] |publisher=[[20th Century Fox]] |location=Beverly Hills, CA |date=2008}}</ref><ref>The date in which the events of ''Alien'' are set is not revealed in the film itself, but the first draft of the script gave the year as 2087. McIntee, 23.</ref>

Sigourney Weaver has expressed interest in reuniting with Ridley Scott to revive her character for another ''Alien'' film. In the 2003 commentary track for the ''Alien'' DVD included in the ''Alien Quadrilogy'' set, she and Scott both speculated on the possibility, with Weaver stating: "There is an appetite for a fifth one, which is something I never expected...it's really hard to come up with a fifth story that's new and fresh...but I have wanted to go back into space...I think outer space adventure is a good thing for us right now, 'cause Earth is so grim...so we've been talking about it, but very generally."<ref name="commentary" /> Scott remarked that, if the series were to continue, the most logical course would be to explore the origins of the space jockey and the aliens.<ref>{{Cite AV media |people=[[Ridley Scott]] (Director) |title=Alien |medium=DVD (audio commentary track) |publisher=[[20th Century Fox]] Home Entertainment, Inc. |date=2003 |quote=It's a tough one, particularly with the success of four. I think if you close the lid it should be the end of the first chapter, and I think very simply what no one's done is simply gone back to re-visit 'what was it?' No one's ever said 'who's the space jockey?' He wasn't an Alien. What was that battleship? Is it a battleship? Is it an aircraft carrier? Is it a bio-mechanoid weapon carrier?...Why did it land? Did it crash-land, or did it settle there because it had engine trouble?...And how long ago? 'Cause those eggs would sit there.}}</ref> Weaver supported this idea, saying "I think it would be great to go back, because I'm asked that question so many times: 'Where did the alien come from?' People really want to know in a very visceral way."<ref name="commentary" /> [[David Giler]] said that he, [[Walter Hill (director)|Walter Hill]], and [[Gordon Carroll]], the producers of the first four films in the series, would not be willing to produce another unless it was about the aliens' homeworld and Weaver was on board (despite the fact that they were among the producers of ''Alien vs. Predator'' films). Weaver indicated that she would only return to the franchise if either Scott or [[James Cameron]] were to direct.<ref name="McIntee, 264">McIntee, 264.</ref> Cameron had been working on a story for a fifth ''Alien'' film which would explore the origins of the creatures, but ceased work on it when he learned that Fox was pursuing ''Alien vs. Predator'', which he felt would "kill the validity of the franchise".<ref name="vespe">{{cite web |last=Vespe |first=Eric "Quint" |title=Holy Crap! Quint Interviews James Cameron!!! |work=[[Ain't It Cool News]] |date=February 7, 2006 |url=https://www.aintitcool.com/display.cgi?id=22405 |access-date=December 20, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071212160208/http://www.aintitcool.com/display.cgi?id=22405 |archive-date=December 12, 2007 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="davidson">{{cite web |last=Davidson |first=Paul |title=AVP Killed Alien 5 |work=[[IGN]] |date=February 8, 2006 |url=http://movies.ign.com/articles/686/686746p1.html |access-date=September 6, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080927181408/http://movies.ign.com/articles/686/686746p1.html |archive-date=September 27, 2008 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In July 2009, 20th Century Fox announced that [[Jon Spaihts]] had been hired to write a prequel to ''Alien'', with Scott attached to direct.<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Fleming |first=Michael |title='Alien' Prequel Takes Off |date=July 30, 2009 |url=https://variety.com/2009/film/markets-festivals/alien-prequel-takes-off-1118006722/ |magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |access-date=August 3, 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090809071708/http://www.variety.com/article/VR1118006722.html?categoryid=13&cs=1 |archive-date=August 9, 2009}}</ref> The script was subsequently re-worked by Scott and [[Damon Lindelof]]. Titled ''[[Prometheus (2012 film)|Prometheus]]'', it went into production in May 2011, and was released the following year. Scott said in a statement: "While ''Alien'' was indeed the jumping-off point for this project, out of the creative process evolved a new, grand mythology and universe in which this original story takes place. The keen fan will recognize strands of ''Alien''{{'s}} DNA, so to speak, but the ideas tackled in this film are unique, large and provocative."<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Abrams |first=Rachel |title=Rapace boards Ridley Scott's ''Prometheus'' |url=https://variety.com/2011/film/news/rapace-boards-ridley-scott-s-prometheus-1118030307/ |url-status=live |magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |date=January 14, 2011 |access-date=June 5, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110118074322/http://www.variety.com/article/VR1118030307 |archive-date=January 18, 2011}}</ref>

''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' reported on February 18, 2015, that a new ''Alien'' film would be developed by [[Neill Blomkamp]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Kroll |first=Justin |title=New 'Alien' Movie Confirmed with Director Neill Blomkamp |url=https://variety.com/2015/film/news/new-alien-movie-confirmed-at-fox-with-director-neill-blomkamp-1201436551/ |url-status=live |work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |date=February 18, 2015 |access-date=February 19, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150219053815/http://variety.com/2015/film/news/new-alien-movie-confirmed-at-fox-with-director-neill-blomkamp-1201436551/ |archive-date=February 19, 2015}}</ref> On February 25, it was confirmed that [[Sigourney Weaver]] would have a role in the film,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://ew.com/article/2015/02/24/neill-blomkamp-alien-chappie-qa/ |title=Neill Blomkamp Q&A: Director talks 'Alien' reboot and new film 'Chappie' |first=Chris |last=Lee |date=February 24, 2015|access-date=September 1, 2022 |publisher=[[Entertainment Weekly]]}}</ref> the intent being to produce a direct sequel to ''Aliens'', ignoring the events of later films, featuring the characters of Hicks and Newt.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.theverge.com/2017/12/30/16832874/neill-blomkamp-canceled-alien-sequel-movie |title=Neill Blomkamp posted some more concept images from his canceled Alien movie |last=Liptak |first=Andrew |work=[[The Verge]] |date=December 30, 2017|access-date=November 22, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181122131851/https://www.theverge.com/2017/12/30/16832874/neill-blomkamp-canceled-alien-sequel-movie|archive-date=November 22, 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> Blomkamp's sequel was ultimately shelved by Fox in favor of ''[[Alien: Covenant]]'', a continuation of Scott's prequel, ''Prometheus''.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/films/news/alien-5-covenant-sir-ridley-scott-sigourney-weaver-neill-blomkamp-sequel-prometheus-prequel-a7712676.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170502155714/http://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/films/news/alien-5-covenant-sir-ridley-scott-sigourney-weaver-neill-blomkamp-sequel-prometheus-prequel-a7712676.html|archive-date=2017-05-02|url-access=limited|url-status= live| title= Alien 5 is doomed as the crew of the Nostromo|last=Stolworthy|first=Jacob|date=May 2, 2017|work=Independent|access-date=June 4, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.ign.com/articles/2017/05/09/alien-covenant-sequel-will-begin-shooting-within-14-months-says-ridley-scott|title=Alien: Covenant Sequel Will Begin Shooting "Within 14 Months", Says Ridley Scott|last=Skrebels|first=Joe|website=[[IGN]]|date=May 9, 2017|access-date=March 6, 2019}}</ref> An eventual fifth ''Alien'' film, ''[[Alien: Romulus]]'', set between the events of ''Alien'' and ''Aliens'', was released in 2024, directed by [[Fede Álvarez]]. A television series titled ''[[Alien: Earth]]'', developed by [[Noah Hawley]], released on streaming on [[Hulu]] in 2025. Several [[computer game]]s [[List of Alien, Predator, and Alien vs. Predator games|based on the film]] were released, but not until several years after its theatrical run.<ref name="McIntee, 39" />
